transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rachel (CTO - Beacon Labs), Samir (ML Eng), Lena (SRE)

Summary (auto):
Quick migration/demo focused on parity mapping for generative API and embeddings, addressing streaming, function calling, and security/VPC questions. Agreement to run a PoC benchmark and get trial keys.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, and with me is Diego our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Rachel: Hi thanks, doing good. Looks like we have about 45 minutes, wanted to make sure we cover the mapping from our current OpenAI + Claude setup to Redwood, and also security questions.
[00:13] Maya: Yeah perfect that's the plan. We'll do a quick product walkthrough — API, Console, and Optimize recommendations — then show how parity mapping works for models and params, and finish with next steps.
[00:23] Diego: Quick note, be aware some transcripts might call our product 'Redwood Optmize' or 'Red wood' in older docs, ignore typos.
[00:28] (laughs)
[00:30] Samir: Cool. For context, we run a mix of OpenAI gpt-4 and gpt-4o for chat, plus Claude 2 for longer context customer-facing workflows. We also use Together embeddings for search. Our main concerns are latency for real-time chat, cost, and keeping data inside our VPC for regulated PII flows.
[00:46] Diego: Got it — that's a familiar stack. We'll show the Redwood API equivalence for chat/generation and embeddings. The mapping is mostly straightforward: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, streaming and function-calling patterns all map 1:1 or with small SDK helpers.
[00:58] Rachel: When you say function-calling, do you support the same JSON schema style like OpenAI's tool call API?
[01:04] Diego: Yes, we have function/tool calling support; the payload is similar. There are slight differences in field names in some older SDKs but our parity doc includes exact cURL and node/python snippets. For streaming, we support chunked HTTP streams and websocket options for low-latency UI.
[01:20] Lena: And how about embeddings? We rely on Together's 1536-d vectors right now. Can we get exact vector dims or do we need to re-index?
[01:29] Maya: Good question. We support multiple embedding flavors; in the parity mapping doc we list matching embedding dims and recommended model equivalents. In some cases you'll need a reindex for small vector size differences; often there are 1:1 equivalents. We'll include recommended quantization and batching params in the doc.
[01:44] Samir: The big thing for us is performance: we need p95 latency under 250ms for chat on short prompts. What are realistic numbers on Redwood hosted vs dedicated?
[01:53] Diego: On hosted our verified performance profile shows p95 ~ 120-200ms for shorter sequences on our curated low-latency models. For your tail-dependent workloads we recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput — Dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and SLA-backed latency. But for initial PoC hosted is simplest. Also we can enable KV prefix cache, which reduces repeated prompt costs and latency for conversation state.
[02:14] Rachel: KV cache — is that something we have to handle or is it automatic?
[02:18] Diego: It's built into the runtime. For persistent sessions you can enable prefix caching per conversation; the API will return a cache token and we handle KV eviction. There are config knobs if you want strict retention windows.
[02:27] Rachel: OK. Security — SOC 2, SSO, KMS? We need details for our security review.
[02:33] Maya: We are SOC 2 Type II. We support SAML SSO/SCIM for RBAC sync and customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. For Dedicated we do network isolation, and Private/VPC deployments give you total control over data plane. We'll attach our security pack and the VPC/on-prem checklist.
[02:49] Lena: For the VPC option do you support air-gapped installs? We may need on-prem for a subset of PII flows.
[02:55] Diego: Yes, we have an on-prem installer that pairs with a private control plane; customers can run inference nodes behind their firewall. We can share the deployment matrix and minimum hardware profile.
[03:06] Samir: Great. Can you show the parity mapping now? Like how a basic OpenAI chat call translates to Redwood SDK?
[03:11] Diego: Sure — demo time. I'll share my screen.
[03:18] [screen share start]
[03:20] Diego: On the left is an example OpenAI request: model gpt-4, messages array, temperature 0.2, max_tokens 800, and a tool call JSON. On the right is Redwood's equivalent: model name is redwood/gpt-4o-llm (example), messages map directly, temperature and max_tokens are the same. For function calling, we use a tools field and specify 'response_mode: tool' if you want the tool result inserted.
[03:47] Maya: Important note — some OpenAI params like presence_penalty/top_p map but may have slightly different defaults; the mapping doc highlights those to avoid unexpected output shifts.
[03:57] Rachel: What about system prompts and instruction tokens? We sometimes rely on system messages to ground behavior. Any differences there?
[04:04] Diego: System messages behave the same; one thing to watch is tokenization differences between models — effective token counts can differ slightly, which affects cost and max length. We recommend running a short tokenization pass during the PoC.
[04:16] Samir: Is there an eval tooling to compare outputs and regressions? We have strict SLAs on hallucination rates.
[04:23] Maya: Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks — you can attach prompt sets and run regression alerts, diff responses across model versions, and track metric changes. We'll demo the console briefly.
[04:32] [screen scroll]
[04:35] Diego: Here's the Console: model catalog, per-route latency and cost breakdowns, and an Optimize suggestions tab that proposes batching and quantization profiles based on your workload. For example, if your average sequence length is 150 tokens, we might recommend a 4-bit quantized variant for non-prod to save cost.
[04:52] Rachel: About quantization — do we need to retrain or does the runtime handle it transparently?
[04:57] Diego: The runtime executes quantized kernels; models are provided in quantized variants we verify, no retraining needed. We do validate quality regressions and suggest fallbacks.
[05:06] Samir: For cost estimation, can we get a per-token parity to our current spend? We want to show finance.
[05:12] Maya: We'll put together a cost comparison sheet in the parity doc — per-token and per-embedding comparisons, plus expected savings from caching and batching. We'll need your current usage numbers to make it accurate.
[05:21] Lena: Any vendor lock-in concerns? If we pin model versions or use dedicated hardware, how portable is our workload?
[05:28] Diego: We provide model versioning and exportable configs. If you pick Private you control the nodes; for Dedicated you can request model artifacts and we provide migration helpers. The API is consistent across deployments so your application code stays the same.
[05:40] Rachel: Let's talk about the Together embeddings replacement — our semantic search pipeline is sensitive, we can't have drift.
[05:46] Diego: For embeddings we recommend a 3-step approach: 1) identify a matching Redwood embedding model with same dims, 2) run a small re-embedding sample (1-5k docs) and compute retrieval metrics, 3) if acceptable, reindex full corpus. We'll share sample scripts.
[05:59] Samir: Awesome. Do you have a recommended benchmark harness? We use a mix of synthetic and production traffic for A/B.
[06:06] Diego: Yes, Diego (me) will share a test harness: concurrent clients, request distributions, latency histograms and token accounting. That will be part of the PoC deliverable.
[06:15] Rachel: Any pitfalls to watch for?
[06:18] Diego: Tokenization differences, function-calling schema mismatches, and embedding dimension mismatches are the usual. We call those out in the parity doc with quick fixes. Also, watch for rate-limit semantics if you migrate from OpenAI rate limits; Redwood supports per-key quotas and per-route throttles.
[06:33] Samir: How does streaming work for web clients? We need to support partial tokens to the browser.
[06:38] Diego: We expose chunked HTTP streaming (server-sent events) and websocket streaming; both integrate with our SDK to give you token-level deltas. In the Console you can toggle streaming and see latency breakdowns.
[06:49] Lena: For our compliance audit, we need audit logs of who called what model and token-level usage. Is that available?
[06:55] Maya: Yes, audit logs, per-token usage, request metadata, and model route tracing are available. For Private deployments customers can ship logs to their SIEM.
[07:05] Rachel: Good. Cost controls — can we set per-route budgets and automatic fallbacks to cheaper models?
[07:11] Diego: Yes, smart routing lets you define policies: e.g., prefer low-cost model, but if latency exceeds threshold, fallback to dedicated variant. You can set per-route budgets and throttles in the Console.
[07:22] Samir: Ok, interested in the PoC. What do you need from us to get started?
[07:26] Maya: We'll need a few things: sample prompts and a small dataset for embeddings, current usage metrics (token counts, embedding volumes), and a list of success criteria (latency p95 targets, cost delta tolerances, quality metrics).
[07:36] Rachel: I'll assign Samir to pull usage numbers and prompt sets.
[07:39] Samir: Yep I'll do that, should have it by Monday.
[07:42] Maya: Great. Final quick recap and action items.
[07:45] Maya: Action items: I'll email the parity mapping doc and quickstart snippets, Diego will set up the benchmark harness and PoC, Samir will share usage. We'll also provision a trial API key and a temporary workspace.
[07:57] Rachel: That sounds good. Any timeline suggestions for the PoC?
[08:00] Diego: Typical PoC runs 2-4 weeks; if you only want performance and cost checks, we can do a focused 1-week benchmark.
[08:08] Rachel: Let's aim for the 1-week focused benchmark first.
[08:11] Maya: Perfect — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Thanks everyone.
[08:15] (call ends)

Notes: transcript includes a few small mis-transcriptions of product names and minor speaker label drift. References made to shared artifacts: "parity mapping doc", "benchmark harness", "security pack (SOC2)" which will be sent after call.

End of transcript.
